newsitem.title: UK: Moving into E Europe? Dig deep for business costs.
newsitem.headline: Moving into E Europe? Dig deep for business costs.

text.p: Starting up business in Warsaw? Expect a three-month wait for a phone. Expanding into Russia? Moscow rents are five times higher than London's. Need a bilingual secretary in Belgrade? Be ready to pay six times what you would in Prague.

So says a new study that compares the costs of setting up business in eastern Europe -- including renting an office, buying a computer, phone charges and a glass of whisky at the end of the day -- with those in London, Paris, Frankfurt and Madrid.

"The DHL Price of Business Index shows that Moscow is by far the most expensive capital for Western business executives," the survey said. "Moscow came out the most expensive city in four of the 10 indicators."
After taking 10 key costs into account for 15 east European capitals, Moscow came out almost three times as expensive as London, followed by Tirana, Ljubjana, Budapest and Kiev.
Kishinev and Bratislava were cheapest, while Skopje, Zagreb, Belgrade, Minsk, Bucharest, Warsaw, Sofia and Prague were in between.
After Moscow, Sofia has the most expensive accomodation for a night in a five star hotel, the survey showed.
Zagreb, Bucharest and Bratislava offer the cheapest office space per square metre, but if you need a phone line, expect to wait 90 days in Warsaw, but only a week in Kiev.
A bilingual secretary in Belgrade gets an average weekly wage of $600, the survey said -- $100 more than in London and six times the salary in Prague.
Desk top computers in Llubjana, Bucharest and Warsaw cost at least double those in Kishinev and Minsk, while the desk itself is three times more expensive in Zagreb as in Bratislava.
And after a hard day's work it is 10 times cheaper to relax in Albania than in Bulgaria -- where a single malt whisky costs $15 compared with $1.50 in Tirana.

Peter Davies, regional director for eastern Europe at DHL Worldwide Express which commissioned the survey, said he was eager to explode some of the myths about setting up business in the former communist east.

"People think if they step outside their hotel they are likely to be arrested by the KGB," he said. "They perceive the people as awkward, the bureaucracy too tough, and that the staff are morose and dressed in grey. It's simply not true," he said.
Muggings and burglaries were no worse than in many cities of the West, he said, while contract killings were rare and blown out of proportion.
Corruption can be avoided by knowing the right person to deal with directly, and knowing how to overcome problems in a legal way, he added.
But certain qualities do help the pioneer business people eager to set up shop in east Europe's renascent economies.
"They need strong communication skills, loads of initiative, independence, strong negotiating skills and bags of empathy in understanding the other person's point of view," Davies said.
"It's never going to be very easy, but it's going to get better as infrastructure improves, facilities get better and governments become more stable," he said.
"There will be a sense of well being among the population and in that environment there will be advantages for industry."
